chunk_findings.detail: The test stubs only `H._stat` (with `chain`), but `_harness` also consults `_wrapper_shell` to decide whether a shell-named ancestor is a `sh -c`-style wrapper (stop/climb). The sibling test `test_a_wrapper_shell_is_climbed_an_interactive_one_is_not` stubs both `_stat` *and* `_wrapper_shell` precisely because of this. Here the real `_wrapper_shell` is left in place, and per `test_which_shells_are_wrappers` it reads the *real* `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. So for the `30: ("bash", 20, "3")` entry, the climb decision is taken from whatever process the host happens to have at pid 30 rather than from the fixture. On a host/container where pid 30 is a wrapper shell (e.g. `/bin/sh -c ...`, a common entrypoint pattern), `_wrapper_shell(30)` returns `True`, `_harness(40)` climbs to the `20` entry, and `H._harness(40) == ["40-4", "30-3"]` fails even though the implementation is correct. chunk_findings.detail:
The change hoists config loading into `renew` (`cfg = Config.load(log.root)` at function entry, plus `cfg.lease.grace_s` inside the new `lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` closure) and simultaneously deletes the only import of `Config` in that function:

```diff
     if ok:
-        from ..config import Config
-        return not _remote_renew(log, Config.load(log.root), item_id, holder, time.time())
+        return not _remote_renew(log, cfg, item_id, holder, time.time())
```

That local import is not redundant cruft: `Config` is deliberately imported lazily in this module (the pre-existing code only imported it inside the `if ok:` branch), whereas names like `Lease`/`EventLog`/`State`/`Item` used in the same file's signatures are module-level. No hunk in this change adds a module-level `from ..config import Config`, so on any call to `renew` the first executable line now evaluates an undefined name and raises `NameError: name 'Config' is not defined` before `_transition` is even reached. Concretely, the environment that triggers it is any running item whose holder heartbeats/renews (the very path the new `refuse` guard was added for): instead of renewing or cleanly returning `False`, the process crashes. The claim-path regression test for B08b6e40bfb does not exercise `renew`, so the breakage is latent even on the fixed code. Restoring a module-level import (or keeping the deferred `from ..config import Config` before the `Config.load` call) is required.

chunk_findings.detail:
The hunk narrows the overlap set from `[*lease.globs, *it.globs]` to `list(lease.globs)`, so the re-claim is now judged only on whatever the lease happened to be pointing at when it lapsed, not on the globs the revived lease will actually cover. The removed comment stated the reason the item's globs had to be included: "the heartbeat's catch-up then points the lease at" them, i.e. after the revive the lease holds `it.globs`. The new comment assumes the catch-up "renews without the ones someone holds now", but the bug scenario this change is supposed to fix falsifies that assumption: B194's re-acquisition at 15:23 covered `store.py` and `api/knowledge.py` while bugfixB's live leases held exactly those files, i.e. the held paths were applied, not dropped.

Concrete failure: take a running item whose lease was acquired before any heartbeat catch-up populated its globs, so `lease.globs == []` (equally, an item that gained a glob while lapsed: `lease.globs == ["a"], it.globs == ["a", "b"]`). Let a live lease from another holder cover `["ddflow/infra/store.py"]`. With `want = list(lease.globs)` the call `glob_clash(state, cfg, it, holder, [], now)` returns `None`, so `lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` returns `False` and the dead lease is revived over files a live lease already holds — two live leases on `store.py`/`api/knowledge.py`, and `ddflow update <other> --globs` refused citing this holder, which is precisely B08b6e40bfb. Before the hunk, `want` included `it.globs`, `glob_clash` found the live lease, and the re-claim was refused. This change makes the function strictly more permissive in the one case (lease globs stale or superset-varying) the bug report turns on.

chunk_findings.detail:
This test mocks only `H._stat` (`chain`) but leaves `H._wrapper_shell` unmocked, while `_harness` classifies ancestor shells through `_wrapper_shell` — the sibling test `test_a_wrapper_shell_is_climbed_an_interactive_one_is_not` patches `_wrapper_shell` for exactly that reason, and `test_which_shells_are_wrappers` shows `_wrapper_shell` reads `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` (it patches `Path.read_bytes` and only special-cases `p.name == "cmdline"`). So when `_harness(40)` reaches the mocked ancestor `30`, it calls the *real* `_wrapper_shell(30)`, i.e. it reads the command line of whatever real process currently has pid 30, not the mocked tuple `("bash", 20, "3")`.

Concretely, the expected `["40-4", "30-3"]` requires `_wrapper_shell(30)` to be `True` (bash is a wrapper shell, so it is included and climbing continues) and `_wrapper_shell(20)` to be `False` (tmux is the interactive terminal boundary, so it is excluded). Against a host where pid 30 does not exist (`Path("/proc/30/cmdline").read_bytes()` raises → error), or exists but is a kernel thread with an empty cmdline / a non-wrapper command (`_wrapper_shell(30) is False` → the loop stops before appending, yielding `["40-4"]`), the assertion fails. The test therefore does not test the intended "don't climb past an interactive shell" rule; its outcome is determined by the ambient process table. It should stub `H._wrapper_shell` (e.g. `lambda pid: pid == 30`) along with `_stat`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard uses "the item already has a lease" (`existing is not None`) as a stand-in for "the item's lease lapsed", but it never tests expiry. The added comment and the appended error text both assert the lease lapsed ("`{item_id}'s lease lapsed and those files were claimed since`"), yet nothing checks `existing.expired(...)`/`expired_at`. The result is that `--force` no longer waives the overlap check for *any* item that already carries a lease, including a still-live one, which is a case the stated reasoning ("expiry freed those files") does not cover. Concrete input: agent A holds a live (non-expired) lease on item X; agent B runs `claim X --force --globs g`, where `g` overlaps item Y's live lease held by agent C. `clash` is non-None, `force` is True, and `existing` is A's live lease, so the call now raises `LeaseError` (with a message claiming X's lease lapsed, which is false) whereas the previous `if clash and not force` completed the forced takeover. If forced takeover of a live lease is meant to keep working, the guard needs to be gated on the existing lease actually being expired (e.g. `existing.expired(now, cfg.lease.grace_s)`), not merely present; as written it changes behaviour for live leases while the message/diagnostic is only valid for the lapsed case.

chunk_findings.detail: The overlap set shrank from the de-duplicated union of `lease.globs` and `it.globs` to `lease.globs` alone. That is the opposite of what the stated fix needs. This predicate is the refusal path for a revival (a live lease "stands"), and the revival ends by pointing the lease at the *item's* globs — the comment that was deleted said exactly that ("the heartbeat's catch-up then points the lease at" them). By dropping `it.globs`, any path the item declares but the expired lease never recorded becomes invisible to `glob_clash`, so it can never trigger a refusal. Concrete input: item X's lease lapses holding `["src/a.py"]`; during the lapse X's globs are set to `["src/a.py", "src/b.py"]`, and holder H2 is granted a live lease on `src/b.py`. Before: `want` contains `src/b.py`, `glob_clash` returns H2's lease, the revival is refused, no double lease. After: `want == ["src/a.py"]`, no clash, the revival is accepted and X holds `src/b.py` while H2's lease is still live — precisely the two-live-leases-on-the-same-file state the bug report describes (kilo-main/B194 re-acquiring `ddflow/api/knowledge.py` while bugfixB/fix-B14d796e03b holds it). The new comment's premise that the catch-up "renews without the ones someone holds now" is the very assumption B08b6e40bfb shows to be false, so this hunk does not close the bug; it removes the item-level overlap detection the bug requires.

chunk_findings.detail: `harness_identity.declared(self.repo)` is keyed only by the repository, and there is nothing process- or agent-specific left to discriminate with (the guard has already established that neither `--agent` nor `DDFLOW_AGENT` is present in this process — that is exactly the condition under which the lookup runs). So in a repo that hosts more than one agent, the first agent to run `ddflow_identify` fixes the declaration, and every later shell of *any* agent in that repo resolves `self.requested_agent` to that same id. Concretely: kilo-main declares itself, then bugfixB runs `ddflow claim/update` in the same repo without `DDFLOW_AGENT` and without `--agent`; `harness_identity.declared(self.repo)` returns "kilo-main", `self.requested_agent` becomes "kilo-main", and `resolve_agent_id` attributes bugfixB's claim and heartbeat to kilo-main. This is exactly the multi-agent situation the fixed bug describes (kilo-main and bugfixB both operating on `ddflow/infra/store.py`, `ddflow/api/knowledge.py`, ...). With both live leases now recorded under the same id, the overlap check treats the other agent's live leases as the holder's own and permits the overlapping re-claim the fix is supposed to prevent. The fix closes the shell-vs-MCP split for a single agent but creates an agent-vs-agent split for any repo shared by two agents.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `if not agent:` branch resolves the connection's identity once, at construction time, from `harness_identity.own(self.repo)` and caches it in `self.agent`. Previously an undeclared connection left `self.agent` empty, which the surrounding comment still documents as "use the process default, the backward-compatible single-agent behaviour" — i.e. the default was resolved downstream, per call. A long-lived MCP server therefore now freezes the identity that was current when the connection was opened. Concretely: a client opens a connection with no `agent` while the harness record names agent A; A's session ends and the harness record is taken over by B; B issues a claim over the same server process. The claim is attributed to A, not B. Because lease/claim ownership is keyed on that identity, this re-creates exactly the failure B08b6e40bfb describes: the re-acquisition is seen as "the holder re-acquiring its own expired running item", so the glob-overlap check against the live leases granted meanwhile is skipped and two live leases can again cover the same files. The same staleness applies when one server process is reused across agents, since `self.agent` is never re-resolved.

chunk_findings.detail: The two arms of the conditional are swapped relative to what `harness_identity.declare` returns. `declare(self.repo, want)` is the call that makes "the same agent's shell commands take it too" (per the Bfad021e8d9 comment), and it hands back the identity the shell now uses; the sibling `else`-branch warning `note += f" Its shell may still use the previous name ({shell})."` confirms `shell` is the name the shell will operate under (truthy = the shell is bound; empty = nothing bound). So a *successful* declaration should read "... , and for its shell", and a *failed* one should read "...; pass --agent to the CLI". As written the logic is inverted: declaring `kilo-main` on the MCP connection (`want` truthy, `declare` returns `"kilo-main"` so `shell` truthy) yields `"declared on this connection; kilo-main: pass --agent to the CLI"`, telling the operator the shell did *not* inherit the agent even though it just did; conversely, when `declare` returns empty (shell could not be bound) the operator is told `"declared on this connection, and for its shell"`, i.e. falsely assured the shell is covered. That second case is exactly the runaway-identity situation the change claims to fix: the operator believes their shell commands carry the declared agent, while in fact their shell will keep deriving/using another identity.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change hoists config loading into `renew` (`cfg = Config.load(log.root)` at function entry, plus `cfg.lease.grace_s` inside the new `lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` closure) and simultaneously deletes the only import of `Config` in that function:

```diff
     if ok:
-        from ..config import Config
-        return not _remote_renew(log, Config.load(log.root), item_id, holder, time.time())
+        return not _remote_renew(log, cfg, item_id, holder, time.time())
```

That local import is not redundant cruft: `Config` is deliberately imported lazily in this module (the pre-existing code only imported it inside the `if ok:` branch), whereas names like `Lease`/`EventLog`/`State`/`Item` used in the same file's signatures are module-level. No hunk in this change adds a module-level `from ..config import Config`, so on any call to `renew` the first executable line now evaluates an undefined name and raises `NameError: name 'Config' is not defined` before `_transition` is even reached. Concretely, the environment that triggers it is any running item whose holder heartbeats/renews (the very path the new `refuse` guard was added for): instead of renewing or cleanly returning `False`, the process crashes. The claim-path regression test for B08b6e40bfb does not exercise `renew`, so the breakage is latent even on the fixed code. Restoring a module-level import (or keeping the deferred `from ..config import Config` before the `Config.load` call) is required.

chunk_findings.detail:
The hunk narrows the overlap set from `[*lease.globs, *it.globs]` to `list(lease.globs)`, so the re-claim is now judged only on whatever the lease happened to be pointing at when it lapsed, not on the globs the revived lease will actually cover. The removed comment stated the reason the item's globs had to be included: "the heartbeat's catch-up then points the lease at" them, i.e. after the revive the lease holds `it.globs`. The new comment assumes the catch-up "renews without the ones someone holds now", but the bug scenario this change is supposed to fix falsifies that assumption: B194's re-acquisition at 15:23 covered `store.py` and `api/knowledge.py` while bugfixB's live leases held exactly those files, i.e. the held paths were applied, not dropped.

Concrete failure: take a running item whose lease was acquired before any heartbeat catch-up populated its globs, so `lease.globs == []` (equally, an item that gained a glob while lapsed: `lease.globs == ["a"], it.globs == ["a", "b"]`). Let a live lease from another holder cover `["ddflow/infra/store.py"]`. With `want = list(lease.globs)` the call `glob_clash(state, cfg, it, holder, [], now)` returns `None`, so `lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` returns `False` and the dead lease is revived over files a live lease already holds — two live leases on `store.py`/`api/knowledge.py`, and `ddflow update <other> --globs` refused citing this holder, which is precisely B08b6e40bfb. Before the hunk, `want` included `it.globs`, `glob_clash` found the live lease, and the re-claim was refused. This change makes the function strictly more permissive in the one case (lease globs stale or superset-varying) the bug report turns on.

chunk_findings.detail:
This test mocks only `H._stat` (`chain`) but leaves `H._wrapper_shell` unmocked, while `_harness` classifies ancestor shells through `_wrapper_shell` — the sibling test `test_a_wrapper_shell_is_climbed_an_interactive_one_is_not` patches `_wrapper_shell` for exactly that reason, and `test_which_shells_are_wrappers` shows `_wrapper_shell` reads `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` (it patches `Path.read_bytes` and only special-cases `p.name == "cmdline"`). So when `_harness(40)` reaches the mocked ancestor `30`, it calls the *real* `_wrapper_shell(30)`, i.e. it reads the command line of whatever real process currently has pid 30, not the mocked tuple `("bash", 20, "3")`.

Concretely, the expected `["40-4", "30-3"]` requires `_wrapper_shell(30)` to be `True` (bash is a wrapper shell, so it is included and climbing continues) and `_wrapper_shell(20)` to be `False` (tmux is the interactive terminal boundary, so it is excluded). Against a host where pid 30 does not exist (`Path("/proc/30/cmdline").read_bytes()` raises → error), or exists but is a kernel thread with an empty cmdline / a non-wrapper command (`_wrapper_shell(30) is False` → the loop stops before appending, yielding `["40-4"]`), the assertion fails. The test therefore does not test the intended "don't climb past an interactive shell" rule; its outcome is determined by the ambient process table. It should stub `H._wrapper_shell` (e.g. `lambda pid: pid == 30`) along with `_stat`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard uses "the item already has a lease" (`existing is not None`) as a stand-in for "the item's lease lapsed", but it never tests expiry. The added comment and the appended error text both assert the lease lapsed ("`{item_id}'s lease lapsed and those files were claimed since`"), yet nothing checks `existing.expired(...)`/`expired_at`. The result is that `--force` no longer waives the overlap check for *any* item that already carries a lease, including a still-live one, which is a case the stated reasoning ("expiry freed those files") does not cover. Concrete input: agent A holds a live (non-expired) lease on item X; agent B runs `claim X --force --globs g`, where `g` overlaps item Y's live lease held by agent C. `clash` is non-None, `force` is True, and `existing` is A's live lease, so the call now raises `LeaseError` (with a message claiming X's lease lapsed, which is false) whereas the previous `if clash and not force` completed the forced takeover. If forced takeover of a live lease is meant to keep working, the guard needs to be gated on the existing lease actually being expired (e.g. `existing.expired(now, cfg.lease.grace_s)`), not merely present; as written it changes behaviour for live leases while the message/diagnostic is only valid for the lapsed case.

chunk_findings.detail: The overlap set shrank from the de-duplicated union of `lease.globs` and `it.globs` to `lease.globs` alone. That is the opposite of what the stated fix needs. This predicate is the refusal path for a revival (a live lease "stands"), and the revival ends by pointing the lease at the *item's* globs — the comment that was deleted said exactly that ("the heartbeat's catch-up then points the lease at" them). By dropping `it.globs`, any path the item declares but the expired lease never recorded becomes invisible to `glob_clash`, so it can never trigger a refusal. Concrete input: item X's lease lapses holding `["src/a.py"]`; during the lapse X's globs are set to `["src/a.py", "src/b.py"]`, and holder H2 is granted a live lease on `src/b.py`. Before: `want` contains `src/b.py`, `glob_clash` returns H2's lease, the revival is refused, no double lease. After: `want == ["src/a.py"]`, no clash, the revival is accepted and X holds `src/b.py` while H2's lease is still live — precisely the two-live-leases-on-the-same-file state the bug report describes (kilo-main/B194 re-acquiring `ddflow/api/knowledge.py` while bugfixB/fix-B14d796e03b holds it). The new comment's premise that the catch-up "renews without the ones someone holds now" is the very assumption B08b6e40bfb shows to be false, so this hunk does not close the bug; it removes the item-level overlap detection the bug requires.

chunk_findings.detail: `harness_identity.declared(self.repo)` is keyed only by the repository, and there is nothing process- or agent-specific left to discriminate with (the guard has already established that neither `--agent` nor `DDFLOW_AGENT` is present in this process — that is exactly the condition under which the lookup runs). So in a repo that hosts more than one agent, the first agent to run `ddflow_identify` fixes the declaration, and every later shell of *any* agent in that repo resolves `self.requested_agent` to that same id. Concretely: kilo-main declares itself, then bugfixB runs `ddflow claim/update` in the same repo without `DDFLOW_AGENT` and without `--agent`; `harness_identity.declared(self.repo)` returns "kilo-main", `self.requested_agent` becomes "kilo-main", and `resolve_agent_id` attributes bugfixB's claim and heartbeat to kilo-main. This is exactly the multi-agent situation the fixed bug describes (kilo-main and bugfixB both operating on `ddflow/infra/store.py`, `ddflow/api/knowledge.py`, ...). With both live leases now recorded under the same id, the overlap check treats the other agent's live leases as the holder's own and permits the overlapping re-claim the fix is supposed to prevent. The fix closes the shell-vs-MCP split for a single agent but creates an agent-vs-agent split for any repo shared by two agents.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `if not agent:` branch resolves the connection's identity once, at construction time, from `harness_identity.own(self.repo)` and caches it in `self.agent`. Previously an undeclared connection left `self.agent` empty, which the surrounding comment still documents as "use the process default, the backward-compatible single-agent behaviour" — i.e. the default was resolved downstream, per call. A long-lived MCP server therefore now freezes the identity that was current when the connection was opened. Concretely: a client opens a connection with no `agent` while the harness record names agent A; A's session ends and the harness record is taken over by B; B issues a claim over the same server process. The claim is attributed to A, not B. Because lease/claim ownership is keyed on that identity, this re-creates exactly the failure B08b6e40bfb describes: the re-acquisition is seen as "the holder re-acquiring its own expired running item", so the glob-overlap check against the live leases granted meanwhile is skipped and two live leases can again cover the same files. The same staleness applies when one server process is reused across agents, since `self.agent` is never re-resolved.

chunk_findings.detail: The two arms of the conditional are swapped relative to what `harness_identity.declare` returns. `declare(self.repo, want)` is the call that makes "the same agent's shell commands take it too" (per the Bfad021e8d9 comment), and it hands back the identity the shell now uses; the sibling `else`-branch warning `note += f" Its shell may still use the previous name ({shell})."` confirms `shell` is the name the shell will operate under (truthy = the shell is bound; empty = nothing bound). So a *successful* declaration should read "... , and for its shell", and a *failed* one should read "...; pass --agent to the CLI". As written the logic is inverted: declaring `kilo-main` on the MCP connection (`want` truthy, `declare` returns `"kilo-main"` so `shell` truthy) yields `"declared on this connection; kilo-main: pass --agent to the CLI"`, telling the operator the shell did *not* inherit the agent even though it just did; conversely, when `declare` returns empty (shell could not be bound) the operator is told `"declared on this connection, and for its shell"`, i.e. falsely assured the shell is covered. That second case is exactly the runaway-identity situation the change claims to fix: the operator believes their shell commands carry the declared agent, while in fact their shell will keep deriving/using another identity.
